clinical_knowledge.topic: NSAID-Induced Gastritis (Functional Dyspepsia) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of NSAID-Induced Gastritis (Functional Dyspepsia) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes stopping NSAIDs if possible, trialling a PPI, and H. pylori test-and-treat, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: burning upper abdominal pain after meals
Key HPI features: epigastric burning pain for 2 months, worse after spicy food and late meals, partial relief with antacids, no weight loss, no black stools, no vomiting blood
Objective/Exam findings: Abdominal exam, weight, stool occult blood if indicated, H. pylori testing.
Current medications: ibuprofen several times per week for back pain
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out NSAID-Induced Gastritis (Functional Dyspepsia).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Gastroesophageal reflux disease without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: haematemesis or melena, unintentional weight loss or early satiety, or sudden severe pain with a rigid abdomen.
management_principles: Stop NSAIDs if possible, trial PPI, H. pylori test-and-treat, safety-net alarm symptoms, consider endoscopy if alarm features or persistent symptoms
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.assessment: Dyspepsia/GERD/gastritis. Consider peptic ulcer disease; assess alarm features.

learning_objectives: Elicit dyspepsia red flags and medication risks
Explain alarm symptoms and endoscopy simply
Address cancer worry without false reassurance

teaching.one_liner: Regular NSAID use irritates and inflames the stomach lining, producing burning upper-abdominal pain after meals without any alarm features of cancer.
red_flags: Haematemesis or melena — suggests a bleeding ulcer rather than uncomplicated gastritis
Unintentional weight loss or early satiety — raises concern for gastric malignancy
Sudden severe pain with a rigid abdomen — suggests perforation

history.answer: Whenever I finish eating, I get this burning, gnawing pain right in the upper pit of my stomach.
It feels like a burning, irritated ache right below my breastbone, and sometimes my stomach feels bloated and heavy.
It is centered right in the epigastric area at the top of my stomach, and it stays there without spreading to my back or chest.
It started about two months ago and has been happening consistently almost every day since.
It definitely gets worse shortly after eating, especially about thirty minutes to an hour after a meal.
It flares up the most when I have spicy dishes or when I eat late at night before going to bed.
I tried taking some over-the-counter liquid antacids, and they help calm the burning down for a little while, but it always comes back.
No, it usually does not wake me up in the middle of the night.
Sometimes I feel a mild burning sensation rising up my chest or a sour taste in my mouth, especially if I lie down right after dinner.
No, my appetite is normal and I do not get full unusually fast.
No, swallowing is completely fine with no food sticking or pain.
No, my weight has been completely steady and I have not lost any weight.
No, I have never thrown up blood or had dark, coffee-ground vomit.
No, my bowel movements look normal brown, with no black, tarry stools or red blood.
I get mild nausea when the burning is bad, but I have not had any actual vomiting.
No, I have not felt dizzy, lightheaded, or unusually tired.
No, I have never had sudden, severe cramping attacks under my right ribs after eating greasy food.
No, the pain does not change when I walk, climb stairs, or exert myself.
I take ibuprofen tablets several times every week because of chronic lower back pain.
I run a restaurant, so my meals are irregular and I often eat late at night, drink three cups of coffee daily, and deal with quite a bit of stress.
I have never had an upper endoscopy before, and I have never been tested or treated for Helicobacter pylori.
I honestly think I have developed severe gastritis from my stress and irregular meals.
My uncle passed away from stomach cancer, so I have been really worried that this burning could be something cancerous.
I am hoping to get proper prescription medicine to stop the burning, and I want to know if I need a stomach endoscopy.
I do not have high blood pressure, diabetes, liver problems, or any other major chronic illnesses.
No, I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
Besides the ibuprofen for my back pain and occasional antacids, I do not take any other prescription medications, aspirin, or supplements.
No, I do not have any known allergies to medications or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I drink about one or two bottles of soju on weekends when relaxing after the restaurant closes.
I own and run a small restaurant, and I live with my wife and two children.
My uncle had stomach cancer, but my parents and siblings are healthy without any chronic medical conditions.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg, pulse is 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 14 breaths per minute, and body temperature is 36.6°C.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor, and sclerae are non-icteric.
No cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, with no palpable Virchow node on the left.
Abdomen is flat and symmetric, with no visible distension, striae, or scars.
Normoactive bowel sounds heard in all four quadrants; no vascular bruits.
Mild tenderness elicited upon deep palpation of the epigastrium; no palpable masses, rigidity, or involuntary guarding.
No rebound tenderness present anywhere in the abdomen.
Negative Murphy's sign without tenderness or inspiratory arrest during deep palpation of the right upper quadrant.
Liver and spleen are not palpable below the costal margins.
Normal sphincter tone with no palpable rectal masses, and stool on the glove is brown and negative for gross blood.
